## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kharassarajātaka* (Ja 79) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection in the Pali Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. In the edition of the *Jātaka* with commentary edited by V. Fausböll, its canonical verse opens with the line *Yato viluttā ca hatā ca gāvo ti* [Fausböll 1877].

The background story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the tale concerning a corrupt minister of the King of Kosala [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The minister, after securing the royal tax collection rights for a border settlement, made a clandestine pact with a gang of robbers: he led the able-bodied villagers into the forest, leaving the settlement defenseless for the bandits to plunder on the condition that they split half of the booty with him [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the treacherous minister of the present with the minister of the past, while the wise man who proclaimed the stanza (*gāthāya udāhārakapaṇḍitamanusso*) was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1877].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan literature [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The text was edited in Roman characters by V. Fausböll in 1877 [Fausböll 1877]. SuttaCentral lists six translations across four languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
